Adaptive Surfing South Africa

By: Jason Boswell | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
a sea of change as disabled surfers take to the waves...

Unique Selling Point:
looking at the world of adaptive surfing after a number of South Africans competed at the recent adaptive surfing championships in La Jolla, California - with one bringing home a gold medal.

Summary:
Caleb Swanepoel lost his leg in a shark attack and has subsequently taken up surfing with a high-tech prosthetic leg. Antony Smyth damaged his right arm severely in a car accident and is one of the pioneers of adaptive surfing in south africa, bringing home a gold medal from the recent Adaptive World Championships in La Jolla California. The story would centre around the two case studies looking at their stories and overcoming the challenges of surfing with their respective disabilities. We will also speak to the South African team's physio who will provide medical viewpoint on how difficult it is to surf for these and other disabled surfers. Additional interviewees would be family members as well as the head of Adaptive Surfing in South Africa.

We will also speak to a young up and coming surfer from the Muizenberg area who is from a disadvantaged background - and talk to them about not only overcoming their social challenges but physical as well and what adaptive surfing means to them.

Further information:
Adaptive Surfing is a unique and seldom covered aspect of surfing in South Africa and the stories of the case studies will highlight the challenges not only from a physical point of view but also to be recognised within the broader surfing community.

Press Release:


Adaptive Surfing
Surfing is one of the most popular water sports in the world and for able bodied swimmers it can be difficult to master. It’s inspired several variations, including windsurfing, wakeboarding and skim boarding, and now adaptive surfing - as surfers with disabilities also take to the waves. Carte Blanche suits up.


Script:


Script Visuals
VO: This stretch of long white sand is renowned as one of the best surf spots in the world…

Short boards…body boards and long boards….all of them enjoy the beautiful breaks here at Muizenberg…

Twenty-two year old UCT student Caleb Swanepoel took up surfing last year…and he’s now just recently back from an international competition in California…but his surfing journey has a slight twist in the tale…

23 seconds – breath in between 2nd and 3rd para.
LINK CLIP0026
Ever since Steven Spielberg asked whether it was safe to go back in the water there’s been an often unhealthy fixation with Great White Sharks. But most of us will never encounter one of these magnificent predators, no matter how long we spend in the water. Sometimes though, our worst nightmares are realised…
UPSOUND Caleb Swanepoel CLIP 0140

“It was a beautiful day, pretty much like today. No wind though, sky clear and everything. So, we headed out for a body surf… And..um..I felt something in the back of my head though, didn’t feel right, something didn’t feel right, and I just felt something slam in to me… I remember trying to hit the shark and trying to push it off my leg, so… but it just, it was locked on, and I just felt it, like, I felt it rip my right leg off…(Caleb Reveal)

I had a moment though, in the water, while this was happening though, where I thought I wasn’t… wasn’t gonna make it, I thought I was gonna die.

Initial Overlay with shots of Caleb surfing…transition to him walking out the water and taking off his wetsuit…focus on prosthetic…
VO: After narrowly surviving his ordeal, Caleb spent 10 days in hospital recovering…As a competitive swimmer he was back in the water within weeks of his attack…
8.5 seconds

LINK: To full appreciate Caleb’s courage it’s important to understand that shark sightings arent actually that rare – particularly here on the False Bay Coast. Infact that red flag behind me is a warning that a shark was spotted off this beach earlier today….
V/O…it was several months later that he discovered something new… 4 seconds

UPSOUND:Caleb Swanepoel: “The first time I stood on a surfboard after my shark attack was with some friends from my gym…

And, I think I got three seconds of balance time on this massive surf board. And that was my first time, that was my first introduction getting back into the water really, with surfing…. And (um) from then on, I came to Muizenberg, and…started surfing…. after that I just had an opportunity to just surf a little contest here at Muizenberg here. And then, also to go overseas and surf as well. “
VO: In December last year Caleb, was part of the South African team which competed at the second World Adaptive Surf Championships in California….

Adaptive Surfers are surfers with disabilities who “adapt” their style or equipment so that they can enjoy the wonderful sport of riding the ocean’s waves.

17 seconds
UPSOUND Antony (CLIP0040) TCR: 06:18…. it’s simple. Surfing isn’t just for able-bodied people. It’s for everybody… 3,5 seconds
V/O Antony Smyth, the South African team’s captain, clinched the gold medal in his division. In addition to being a world champion, Antony also serves as Chairman of Adaptive Surfing South Africa… 10 seconds
UPSOUND Antony Smyth

We are trying to make it easier, for people with disabilities to go surfing. That could be me. You know, I don’t need much help, I’ve got two legs, I can walk around, and walk to the beach. But a person in a wheelchair needs a way to get into the water: help, equipment.

(02:11)

“…surfing is a cool sport to start off with..When they’re in the water, they free. They can paddle, if they wanna go there they can go there. They are the same. The sea is a leveller. And that’s the great thing about adaptive surfing Visuals of Antony kitting up and getting ready to surf Llandudno…


VO: Surfing is still something new for Caleb, and between university and home, it can be tricky fitting it all in… 6 seconds
UPSOUND CLIP0144 (01:15) Caleb:

“…if I get up early enough I’ll go for a swim at Sport Science – or, I’ll go for a terrain session at the gym. So those two things work hand in hand. Then, it’s quite a long day at varsity, so, usually the day will start at nine/ten o’clock, at varsity, so a lecture on upper campus at UCT, and then practical throughout the afternoon at, on Hilling campus. And, I stay with my siblings, so, we all have different evenings for supper…

UPSOUND JOHN

“So your family doesn’t let you catch a break do they? You’ve still got to do your chores?”

UPSOUND CALEB

“I’ve still gotta do my chores my sister keeps me in check, she’s also studying with me, so, I mean, if you wash your stuff and you… you can’t just leave it in the sink it must be done

“ …just having my family in Cape Town I think I’ve been really lucky, because they also keep me in check, don’t let me get too, too, cocky or anything like that. (Um) and tell me when I’ve done enough talking, because apparently, I like to do a lot of talking as well…”
LINK: Perhaps it’s because it’s the perfect synery between humans and nature or the fact that when it’s done properly it’s poetry in motion – whatever the reason on face value, surfing doesn’t appearing particulalty taxing or technical…when in fact the opposite is true…
Visuals of surfing…approximately (5 seconds) seconds… Music here…
UPSOUND: CLIP0146 – John
“Surfing is an incredibly technical sport, even for able-bodied people – so how dificult has it been for you to get up and surf?
UPSOUND Caleb (Clip0142) 07:32:

“It’s still frustrating sometimes…especially when the waves are small, or if they too big, because, there’s a lot of factors that affect the prosthetic in the water..it’s not designed for surfing per se, so it doesn’t bend like a normal leg when it’s in the water

…you manoeuver with the front part of your body, so, my manoeuvrability has to come more from my upper body.So that is a hinderance yes…”
Underwater shot of Caleb on his board with prosthetic…Caleb walking out the water and taking his wetsuit off…(focus on prosthetic shots)

V/O It’s technical difficulties such as these that physiotherapist Helen Millson is hoping to be able to assist with….
6.5 seconds
UPSOUND Helen Millson (CLIP0016) (00:14)

“…They might have a physical impairment, but so has everybody who comes in to see me, so it’s about how to make them better, stronger…
Overlay
…having worked with world championship teams in several sports she’s already been impressed by the adaptive surfers… 6.5 seconds

UPSOUND Helen Millson

…he’s brilliant, he’s fantastic. but, fine tuning to make him the best, is the balance, co-ordination, plus all the rest...

…I’ve been moved by so many things (interviewer: ‘hmm’), um, I’m passionate about a lot of things, but I would say this probably has moved me beyond all.”

B-Roll of Caleb and Helen.

(Shots of Caleb at gym – box jumps)

LINK CLIP 0029 (last take)
Still in its infancy, Adaptive Surfing is showing tremendous promise not only as a competitive sport – but also as a type of therapy for people who’ve experienced significant trauma in their lives… Overlay with surf footage
VO: Paul Jurgens is a volunteer who helps introduce people into the world of adaptive surfing…. 5,5 seconds
UPSOUND…John, “how important do you think it do you think it’s going to become…how important as a tool do you think it’s going to become…”

““I’m hoping that it’s gonna take off quite well, because, (um), what I find is that water is very healing.”

…any person…being in a wheelchair it’s very healing…

“…when they go in the water and they come out, there’s just smiling, and they just smile. And they just, feel so welcome and happy.”
Shots of Nolo in the water….


V/O One of the people who Paul has recently helped introduce into adapative surfing is Nolo Mbane, who has cerebral palsy, but there’s no hiding her excitement… 9 seconds
UPSOUND CLIP0006 Nolo Mbane

“I like surfing, very very much…”

John, “what do you like about it…”

“Because it’s nice and the water is…wowing…and the dog is very nice…”


VO: People with disabilities have been surfing for years and while it’s only recently that Adapative Surfing has emerged as an officially recognised competitive sport, with people like Antony claiming world championships and young up-and-coming surfers like Caleb learning the waves…they hope the Adaptive Surfing will have a bright future in South Africa…

And while competitions and world championships are great goals to aspire to…it’s not just about that…


25,5 seconds
UPSOUND CLIP 0142 (09:54)

“ I think I can definitely push it further in terms of competitive sports. So, my aim is to get a surfing leg, which will be hopefully this year…it’ll be lighter, it’ll be angled. It won’t look too pretty walking out into the waves ‘cause it won’t bend, but once I’m out there I can ride a shorter board…and just enjoy the ride.”


Promos
15 Seconds
1.) VO: Surfing is a pretty tough…now imagine trying to surf…competitively…without an arm or a leg…. (6 seconds)
UPSOUND – Caleb Swanepoel “It’s still frustrating sometimes… there’s a lot of factors that affect the prosthetic in the water.”
2.) UPSOUND Antony Smyth: “it’s simple. Surfing isn’t just for able-bodied people. It’s for everybody…”
VO: South Africa’s disabled surfers adapt their style and equipment to take on the waves… (5,5 seconds)

15 seconder
South Africa’s disabled surfers have been taking to the water for years, and while it’s only recently that Adaptive Surfing has been recognised an official sport…the country’s surfers are already making waves… (10,5 seconds)
